title: BridgeKit: carry the learning forward
reason: We're switching to paper and spoken contributions so everyone can take part without a reliable phone or data connection.
story: A phone-access barrier changes a workshop activity. The next facilitator receives the plan, its history, and the reason for the change.

stages.title: Frame the challenge
actions: Begin inside the sample workshop on Plan, with v1 visible.
Point to Ideas in the open. Keep the opening focused on the challenge.
stages.say: BRIDGEGOOD's Design for Social Good mindset grows through people, mentorship, and relationships. As the organization scales, that knowledge needs to travel beyond any one person. BridgeKit helps a facilitator practice the philosophy in a workshop, act on feedback, and pass the learning to the next community.
stages.proof: The unit of sharing is a workshop with its reasoning and learning.

stages.title: Make the reasoning teachable
actions: Scroll within the page and open Why it helps and Participation options.
Point to the reason and Hack Pack source links. Keep source pages for Q&A.
stages.say: I'm starting with a fictional campus workshop. Each activity carries instructions, the reason behind them, a BRIDGEGOOD source, and another way to participate. The next facilitator can explain why the activity exists, then adapt it for the people in their room. That makes the philosophy practical and teachable.
stages.proof: BRIDGEGOOD's reasoning and attribution are connected to an activity people can practice.

stages.title: Listen to an access barrier
actions: Click Listen in the step bar, or Next: listen.
Find the first Barrier card about phone or data access.
Read its observation, then click Respond on that card.
stages.say: Now let's test the plan against the people using it. This demo feedback says the digital board was hard to join without a reliable phone or data connection. That is a concrete access barrier. I'll respond by deciding what needs to change.
stages.proof: Community experience becomes the trigger for a facilitator decision.

stages.title: Make and explain a choice
actions: Review Change activity and Start from: Paper-first idea studio. Both are already selected for this sample barrier.
Scroll inside the dialog to Why this choice?, and paste the prepared reason.
Click Save change. Confirm the card now says Adapted.
stages.say: BridgeKit asks the facilitator to make a choice. I'm choosing Paper-first idea studio, where people can sketch, write, dictate, or speak without a phone. I'll record the reason: we are changing the format so everyone can contribute without reliable phone data. We could also keep an activity and explain why. The facilitator stays in control; the tool preserves the decision and its reasoning.
stages.proof: A human chooses the adaptation and explains why it fits this group.

stages.title: Show what changed
actions: Scroll to the step bar and click Share.
Scroll to What changed. Point to the original activity, the paper activity, and Why it changed.
Click Version history; point to v1 Original and v2 Feedback. Close the dialog.
stages.say: Here is the result: the digital activity becomes a paper activity, and the reason is visible beside the change. Version history keeps the original plan. We are passing on a way to make thoughtful decisions, so the next facilitator can understand the choice and respond to their own group.
stages.proof: Learning is visible, and the original remains available.

stages.title: Carry the learning forward
actions: Scroll to Share your kit and click Download kit.
Scroll to the top bar and click Import kit. Select the just-downloaded a-more-welcoming-campus-bridgekit JSON file; duplicate filenames may have a number suffix.
Confirm the new workshop has Paper-first idea studio and v2. Keep the extra Listen check for Q&A if time is tight.
stages.say: I'll download the kit and import it as a new workshop, simulating a handoff to another facilitator. The revised activity and its history come with it. Raw feedback is excluded; reasons and edited instructions still need review before sharing. The next community gets a useful starting point and room to make its own choices.
stages.proof: An actual export/import carries the revised plan and history to a new workshop.

stages.title: Close with the pilot question
actions: Stop clicking and look at the audience.
Finish on the imported plan. Emphasize the next facilitator and the pilot.
stages.say: Our answer to scaling BRIDGEGOOD is to carry the mindset through decisions people can explain and improve. This is a working browser prototype with draft activities. Next, we want BRIDGEGOOD's review and a pilot testing whether a new facilitator can use a kit independently, and whether participants have meaningful ways to take part.
stages.proof: The next milestone is useful independent reuse, evaluated with the community.

prepare: Use a desktop-width window. Start the app with npm run dev and open the address Vite prints.
Click Try a sample in the left sidebar. Confirm v1, Ideas in the open, and an open phone-data Barrier in Listen; return to Plan.
Keep the sample context unchanged. Selecting Limited internet before rebuilding would start with paper and remove the before/after story.
Copy the prepared reason before presenting. Scroll inside the response dialog to reach the reason and Save change.
Rehearse download/import once and leave the file picker in Downloads. During the live demo, choose the newest exported kit.
After a completed practice, click Try a sample to open an unadapted sample or create one. Confirm v1 before the next run.
fallback: At 2:50, move to sharing. The v1/v2 rows are enough; save opening every historical activity for Q&A.
If the file picker stalls, close it and use the imported-plan screenshot. Say: 'This is the imported example from our rehearsal.'
At 3:30, stop clicking and deliver the closing. Keep setup, library browsing, print dialogs, and technical details for Q&A.
Keep the PDF and 75-second captioned demo locally available as backups.

faq.question: Why does this address the challenge?
faq.answer: It connects BRIDGEGOOD's reasoning to practice, makes feedback decisions explainable, and passes that learning to another facilitator.

faq.question: Is there AI or a backend?
faq.answer: The MVP uses deterministic planning rules and browser localStorage. Facilitators choose adaptations. Accounts, shared sessions, and cloud synchronization are future work.

faq.question: What is protected when a kit is shared?
faq.answer: Raw reflection records are excluded, and handoff notes start excluded. Context, decision reasons, and edited activity text are shared, so facilitators review them before exporting.

faq.question: What impact has been measured?
faq.answer: The current evidence is a working prototype and verified handoff. A pilot should test independent facilitator reuse, useful feedback decisions, and participant choice. Community outcomes have not yet been measured.

faq.question: Why are two feedback items still open?
faq.answer: The four-minute demo completes one decision. The remaining feedback stays visible for review; the kit is an evolving draft.

faq.question: Are these official BRIDGEGOOD materials?
faq.answer: They are draft hackathon adaptations connected to the Hack Pack. BRIDGEGOOD review is a next step.
